newsitem.title: CHILE: Analysts see rough weather ahead for copper prices.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see rough weather ahead for copper prices.

text.p: Rising copper output in Latin America and elsewhere may outpace growth in demand over the next few years, causing the price to wobble downwards, industry officials and analysts said Friday at a copper conference.
Standard and Poor's corporate ratings director Dmitri Nayduch told the conference in Chile that a likely global economic slowdown will also take some shine off the red metal.
"I don't think it takes really draconian projections to see the possibility of much lower copper prices in the next few years," Nayduch said.

He explained "It's been about four years since there's been a global recession and some time in the next couple of years there's a fairly high likelihood that there could be another recession, ...and so on the demand side you could be facing a reduction..."

Nayduch forecast tougher environmental restrictions and accelerating trends to larger mining companies and lower cost production, which he said could make the copper market swing more wildly than before.

"The other issue is that a lot of these big projects are extremely low cost, at 35, 40 cents per pound. If they meet these projections there could be a reduction...in the cost curve which could result in greater volatility in copper prices."

But generally, increasing demand in industrialising countries for copper goods and higher consumption of electronics in rich parts of the world should be able to cope with higher output. Nayduch said that this new demand should also compensate for the substitution of some copper demand with newer technology like optical fiber.
But another conference delegate cautioned that one of the main hopes for future copper market, Asia, may not prove as ravenous for the metal as some hope.

"Many people believe Asian refined copper consumption will grow and grow and grow, but it depends on the world economy," Tadaaki Ezawa, senior analyst of Japan's industry-funded Metal Economics Research Institute, told Reuters.
"Copper consumption in Asia is expanding continually but it depends on the world economy, especially in my opinion on the U.S. economy," he said.
He said that Japanese consumption of refined copper should remain stable at about 1.6 million tonnes a year, at least for the remaining years of the century.
"After that I don't know. The reason I cannot predict Japanese copper consumption is technical innovation."
But Ezawa said that another source of demand may come from Latin America, where most of the new mines are being built.

"I think that in the near future Latin America's industrialising countries will expand their consumption of refined copper, in Brazil, Argentina, Chile. There is a big potential in Latin America to use refined copper," he said.

John Gross, strategic metals vice-president for Britain's BICC Cables also warned the conference that copper prices may be heading for the low part of the cycle. This would mean that some mines now on the drawing board may be scrapped.
"The economics will prevent all the projects coming on stream," he said.
